entries.bf031ce62bac11cb55c894bbe63fe2b194f399a3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7"/><title type="x-ms">Deuteronomy</title> <div sID="gen3353" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen3353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3354" type="x-p"/> <hi type="small-caps">This</hi> book is a repetition of very much both of the history and of the laws contained in the three foregoing books, which repetition Moses delivered to Israel (both by word of mouth, that it might affect, and by writing, that it might abide) a little before his death. There is no new history in it but that of the death of Moses in the last chapter, nor any new revelation to Moses, for aught that appears, and therefore the style here is not, as before, <hi type="italic">The Lord spoke unto Moses, saying.</hi> But the former laws are repeated and commented upon, explained and enlarged, and some particular precepts added to them, with copious reasonings for the enforcing of them: in this Moses was divinely inspired and assisted, so that this is as truly the word of the Lord by Moses as that which was spoken to him with an audible voice <hi type="italic">out of the tabernacle of the congregation</hi>, <reference osisRef="Lev.1.1">Lev. i. 1</reference>. The Greek interpreters call it <hi type="italic">Deuteronomy,</hi> which signifies the <hi type="italic">second law,</hi> or a <hi type="italic">second edition of the law,</hi> not with amendments, for there needed none, but with additions, for the further direction of the people in divers cases not mentioned before. Now, I. It was much for the honour of the divine law that it should be thus repeated; how great were the things of that law which was thus inculcated, and how inexcusable would those be by whom they were <hi type="italic">counted as a strange thing!</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.8.12">Hos. viii. 12</reference>. II. There might be a particular reason for the repeating of it now; the men of that generation to which the law was first given were all dead, and a new generation had sprung up, to whom God would have it repeated by Moses himself, that, if possible, it might make a lasting impression upon them. Now that they were just going to take possession of the land of Canaan, Moses must read the articles of agreement to them, that they might know upon what terms and conditions they were to hold and enjoy that land, and might understand that they were upon their good behaviour in it. III. It would be of great use to the people to have those parts of the law thus gathered up and put together which did more immediately concern them and their practice; for the laws which concerned the priests and Levites, and the execution of their offices, are not repeated: it was enough for them that they were once delivered. But, in compassion to the infirmities of the people, the laws of more common concern are delivered a second time. <hi type="italic">Precept must be upon precept, and line upon line,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.28.10">Isa. xxviii. 10</reference>. The great and needful truths of the gospel should be often pressed upon people by the ministers of Christ. <hi type="italic">To write the same things</hi> (says Paul, <reference osisRef="Phil.3.1">Phil. iii. 1</reference>) <hi type="italic">to me indeed is not grievous, but for you it is safe.</hi> What God has spoken once we have need to hear twice, to hear many times, and it is well if, after all, it be duly perceived and regarded. In three ways this book of Deuteronomy was magnified and made honourable:— 1. The king was to write a copy of it with his own hand, and to read therein all the days of his life, <reference osisRef="Deut.17.1-Deut.19.21">ch. xvii. xviii. xix.</reference> 2. It was to be written upon great stones plastered, at their passing over Jordan, <reference osisRef="Deut.27.2-Deut.27.3">ch. xxvii. 2, 3</reference>. 3. It was to be read publicly every seventh year, at the feast of tabernacles, by the priests, in the audience of all Israel, <reference osisRef="Deut.31.9-Deut.31.13">ch. xxxi. 9</reference>, &c. The gospel is a kind of Deuteronomy, a second law, a remedial law, a spiritual law, a law of faith; by it we are under the law of Christ, and it is a law that <hi type="italic">makes the comers thereunto perfect.</hi> <div eID="gen3354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3355" type="x-p"/> This book of Deuteronomy begins with a brief rehearsal of the most remarkable events that had befallen the Israelites since they came from Mount Sinai. In the fourth chapter we have a most pathetic exhortation to obedience. In the twelfth chapter, and so on to the twenty-seventh, are repeated many particular laws, which are enforced (<reference osisRef="Deut.27.1-Deut.28.68">ch. xxvii. and xxviii.</reference>) with promises and threatenings, blessings and curses, formed into a covenant, <reference osisRef="Deut.29.1-Deut.30.20">ch. xxix. and xxx.</reference> Care is taken to perpetuate the remembrance of these things among them (<reference osisRef="Deut.31.1-Deut.31.29">ch. xxxi.</reference>), particularly by a song (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.1-Deut.32.52">ch. xxxii.</reference>), and so Moses concludes with a blessing, <reference osisRef="Deut.33.1-Deut.33.29">ch. xxxiii</reference>. All this was delivered by Moses to Israel in the last month of his life. The whole book contains the history but of two months; compare <reference osisRef="Deut.1.3">ch. i. 3</reference> with <reference osisRef="Josh.4.19">Josh. iv. 19</reference>, the latter of which was the thirty days of Israel's mourning for Moses; see how busy that great and good man was to do good when he knew that his time was short, how quick his motion when he drew near his rest. Thus we have more recorded of what our blessed Saviour said and did in the last week of his life than in any other. The last words of eminent persons make or should make deep impressions. Observe, for the honour of this book, that when our Saviour would answer the devil's temptations with, <hi type="italic">It is written,</hi> he fetched all his quotations out of this book, <reference osisRef="Matt.4.4">Matt. iv. 4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.4.7">7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.4.10">10</reference>. <div eID="gen3355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3356" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen3357" type="x-p"/> The first part of Moses's farewell sermon to Israel begins with this chapter, and is continued to the latter end of the fourth chapter. In the first five verses of this chapter we have the date of the sermon, the place where it was preached (<reference osisRef="Deut.1.1-Deut.1.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.1.5">5</reference>), and the time when, <reference osisRef="Deut.1.3-Deut.1.4">ver. 3, 4</reference>. The narrative in this chapter reminds them, I. Of the promise God made them of the land of Canaan, <reference osisRef="Deut.1.6-Deut.1.8">ver. 6-8</reference>. II. Of the provision made of judges for them, <reference osisRef="Deut.1.9-Deut.1.18">ver. 9-18</reference>. III. Of their unbelief and murmuring upon the report of the spies, <reference osisRef="Deut.1.19-Deut.1.33">ver. 19-33</reference>. IV. Of the sentence passed upon them for it, and the ratification of that sentence, <reference osisRef="Deut.1.34-Deut.1.46">ver. 34</reference>, &c. <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7"/> <div eID="gen3357" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen3356" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Israel's History Repeated. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1451.)</title> <div sID="gen3358" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> These <hi type="italic">be</hi> the words which Moses spake unto all Israel on this side Jordan in the wilderness, in the plain over against the Red <hi type="italic">sea,</hi> between Paran, and Tophel, and Laban, and Hazeroth, and Dizahab. <hi type="super">2</hi> (<hi type="italic">There are</hi> eleven days' <hi type="italic">journey</hi> from Horeb by the way of mount Seir unto Kadesh-barnea.) <hi type="super">3</hi> And it came to pass in the fortieth year, in the eleventh month, on the first <hi type="italic">day</hi> of the month, <hi type="italic">that</hi> Moses spake unto the children of Israel, according unto all that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> had given him in commandment unto them; <hi type="super">4</hi> After he had slain Sihon the king of the Amorites, which dwelt in Heshbon, and Og the king of Bashan, which dwelt at Astaroth in Edrei: <hi type="super">5</hi> On this side Jordan, in the land of Moab, began Moses to declare this law, saying, <hi type="super">6</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> our God spake unto us in Horeb, saying, Ye have dwelt long enough in this mount: <hi type="super">7</hi> Turn you, and take your journey, and go to the mount of the Amorites, and unto all <hi type="italic">the places</hi> nigh thereunto, in the plain, in the hills, and in the vale, and in the south, and by the sea side, to the land of the Canaanites, and unto Lebanon, unto the great river, the river Euphrates. <hi type="super">8</hi> Behold, I have set the land before you: go in and possess the land which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> sware unto your fathers, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, to give unto them and to their seed after them. <div eID="gen3358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3359" type="x-p"/> We have here, I. The date of this sermon which Moses preached to the people of Israel. A great auditory, no question, he had, as many as could crowd within hearing, and particularly all the elders and officers, the representatives of the people; and, probably, it was on the sabbath day that he delivered this to them. 1. The place were they were now encamped was <hi type="italic">in the plain, in the land of Moab</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.1.1">v. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.1.5">5</reference>), where they were just ready to enter Canaan, and engage in a war with the Canaanites. Yet he discourses not to them concerning military affairs, the arts and stratagems of war, but concerning their duty to God; for, if they kept themselves in his fear and favour, he would secure to them the conquest of the land: their religion would be their best policy. 2. The time was near the end of the fortieth year since they came out of Egypt. So long God had <hi type="italic">borne their manners,</hi> and they had <hi type="italic">borne their own iniquity</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.14.34">Num. xiv. 34</reference>), and now that a new and more pleasant scene was to be introduced, as a token for good, Moses repeats the law to them. Thus, after God's controversy with them on account of the golden calf, the first and surest sign of God's being reconciled to them was the <hi type="italic">renewing of the tables.</hi> There is no better evidence and earnest of God's favour than his putting his law in our hearts, <reference osisRef="Ps.147.19-Ps.147.20">Ps. cxlvii. 19, 20</reference>. <div eID="gen3359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3360" type="x-p"/> II. The discourse itself. In general, Moses spoke unto them <hi type="italic">all that the Lord had given him in commandment</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.1.3">v. 3</reference>), which intimates, not only that what he now delivered was for substance the same with what had formerly been commanded, but that it was what God now commanded him to repeat. He gave them this rehearsal and exhortation purely by divine direction; God appointed him to leave this legacy to the church. He begins his narrative with their removal from Mount Sinai (<reference osisRef="Deut.1.6">v. 6</reference>), and relates here, 1. The orders which God gave them to decamp, and proceed in their march (<reference osisRef="Deut.1.6-Deut.1.7">v. 6, 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">You have dwelt long enough in this mount.</hi> This was the mount <hi type="italic">that burned with fire</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.18">Heb. xii. 18</reference>), and <hi type="italic">gendered to bondage,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.4.24">Gal. iv. 24</reference>. Thither God brought them to humble them, and by the terrors of the law to prepare them for the land of promise. There he kept them about a year, and then told them they had <hi type="italic">dwelt long enough</hi> there, they must go forward. Though God brings his people into trouble and affliction, into spiritual trouble and affliction of mind, he knows when they have dwelt long enough in it, and will certainly find a time, the fittest time, to advance them from the terrors of the spirit of adoption. See <reference osisRef="Rom.8.15">Rom. viii. 15</reference>. 2. The prospect which he gave them of a happy and early settlement in Canaan: <hi type="italic">Go to the land of the Canaanites</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.1.7">v. 7</reference>); enter and take possession, it is all your own. <hi type="italic">Behold I have set the land before you,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.1.8">v. 8</reference>. When God commands us to go forward in our Christian course he sets the heavenly Canaan before us for our encouragement.
entries.0602344e402a7b63c1bd49444736572e15e246b8: <div eID="gen3360" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Charge to Magistrates. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1451.)</title> <div sID="gen3361" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> And I spake unto you at that time, saying, I am not able to bear you myself alone: <hi type="super">10</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God hath multiplied you, and, behold, ye <hi type="italic">are</hi> this day as the stars of heaven for multitude. <hi type="super">11</hi> (The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of your fathers make you a thousand times so many more as ye <hi type="italic">are,</hi> and bless you, as he hath promised you!) <hi type="super">12</hi> How can I myself alone bear your cumbrance, and your burden, and your strife? <hi type="super">13</hi> Take you wise men, and understanding, and known among your tribes, and I will make them rulers over you. <hi type="super">14</hi> And ye answered me, and said, The thing which thou hast spoken <hi type="italic">is</hi> good <hi type="italic">for us</hi> to do. <hi type="super">15</hi> So I took the chief of your tribes, wise men, and known, and made them heads over you, captains over thousands, and captains over hundreds, and captains over fifties, and captains over tens, and officers among your tribes. <hi type="super">16</hi> And I charged your judges at that time, saying, Hear <hi type="italic">the causes</hi> between your brethren, and judge righteously between <hi type="italic">every</hi> man and his brother, and the stranger <hi type="italic">that is</hi> with him. <hi type="super">17</hi> Ye shall not respect persons in judgment; <hi type="italic">but</hi> ye shall hear the small as well as the great; ye shall not be afraid of the face of man; for the judgment <hi type="italic">is</hi> God's: and the cause that is too hard for you, bring <hi type="italic">it</hi> unto me, and I will hear it. <hi type="super">18</hi> And I commanded you at that time all the things which ye should do. <div eID="gen3361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3362" type="x-p"/> Moses here reminds them of the happy constitution of their government, which was such as might make them all safe and easy if it was not their own fault. When good laws were given them good men were entrusted with the execution of them, which, as it was an instance of God's goodness to them, so it was of the care of Moses concerning them; and, it should seem, he mentions it here to recommend himself to them as a man that sincerely sought their welfare, and so to make way for what he was about to say to them, wherein he aimed at nothing but their good. In this part of his narrative he insinuates to them, <div eID="gen3362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3363" type="x-p"/> I. That he greatly rejoiced in the increase of their numbers. He owns the accomplishment of God's promise to Abraham (<reference osisRef="Deut.1.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">You are as the stars of heaven for multitude;</hi> and prays for the further accomplishment of it (<reference osisRef="Deut.1.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">God make you a thousand times more.</hi> This prayer comes in in a parenthesis, and a good prayer prudently put in cannot be impertinent in any discourse of divine things, nor will a pious ejaculation break the coherence, but rather strengthen and adorn it. But how greatly are his desires enlarged when he prays that they might be made a thousand times more than they were! We are not straitened in the power and goodness of God, why should we be straitened in our own faith and hope, which ought to be as large as the promise? larger they need not be. It is from the promise that Moses here takes the measures of his prayer: <hi type="italic">The Lord bless you as he hath promised you.</hi> And why might he not hope that they might become a thousand times more than they were now when they were now ten thousand times more than they were when they went down into Egypt, about 250 years ago? Observe, When they were under the government of Pharaoh the increase of their numbers was envied, and complained of as a grievance (<reference osisRef="Exod.1.9">Exod. i. 9</reference>); but now, under the government of Moses, it was rejoiced in, and prayed for as a blessing. The consideration of this might give them occasion to reflect with shame upon their own folly when they had talked of making a captain and returning to Egypt. <div eID="gen3363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3364" type="x-p"/> II. That he was not ambitious of monopolizing the honour of the government, and ruling them himself alone, as an absolute monarch, <reference osisRef="Deut.1.9">v. 9</reference>. Though he was a man as well worthy of that honour, and as well qualified for the business, as ever any man was, yet he was desirous that others might be taken in as assistants to him in the business and consequently sharers with him in the honour: <hi type="italic">I cannot myself alone bear the burden,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.1.12">v. 12</reference>. Magistracy is a burden. Moses himself, though eminently gifted for it, found it lay heavily on his shoulders; nay, the best magistrates complain most of the burden, and are most desirous of help, and most afraid of undertaking more than they can perform. <div eID="gen3364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3365" type="x-p"/> III. That he was not desirous to prefer his own creatures, or such as should underhand have a dependence upon him; for he leaves it to the people to choose their own judges, to whom he would grant commissions, not <hi type="italic">durant bene placito—to be turned out when he pleased;</hi> but <hi type="italic">quam diu se bene gesserint—to continue so long as they approved themselves faithful. Take you wise men, that are known to be so among your tribes, and I will make them rulers,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.1.13">v. 13</reference>. Thus the apostles directed the multitude to choose overseers of the poor, and then they ordained them,. <reference osisRef="Acts.6.3">Acts vi. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.6.6">6</reference>. He directs them to <hi type="italic">take wise men and understanding,</hi> whose personal merit would recommend them. The rise and origin of this nation were so late that none of them could pretend to antiquity of race, and nobility of birth, above their brethren; and, having all lately come out of slavery in Egypt, it is probable that one family was not much richer than another; so that their choice must be directed purely by the qualifications of wisdom, experience, and integrity. "Choose those," says Moses, "whose praise is in your tribes, and with all my heart <hi type="italic">I will make them rulers.</hi>" We must not grudge that God's work be done by other hands than ours, provided it be done by good hands. <div eID="gen3365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3366" type="x-p"/> IV. That he was in this matter very willing to please the people; and, though he did not in any thing aim at their applause, yet in a thing of this nature he would not act without their approbation. And they agreed to the proposal: <hi type="italic">The thing which thou hast spoken is good,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.1.14">v. 14</reference>. This he mentions to aggravate the sin of their mutinies and discontents after this, that the government they quarrelled with was what they themselves had consented to; Moses would have pleased them if they would have been pleased. <div eID="gen3366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3367" type="x-p"/> V. That he aimed to edify them as well as to gratify them; for, <div eID="gen3367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3368" type="x-p"/> 1. He appointed men of good characters (<reference osisRef="Deut.1.15">v. 15</reference>), <hi type="italic">wise men and men known,</hi> men that would be faithful to their trust and to the public interest. <div eID="gen3368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3369" type="x-p"/> 2. He gave them a good charge, <reference osisRef="Deut.1.16-Deut.1.17">v. 16, 17</reference>. Those that are advanced to honour must know that they are charged with business, and must give account another day of their charge. (1.) He charges them to be diligent and patient: <hi type="italic">Hear the causes.</hi> Hear both sides, hear them fully, hear them carefully; for nature has provided us with two ears, and <hi type="italic">he that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame to him.</hi> The ear of the learner is necessary to the tongue of the learned, <reference osisRef="Isa.50.4">Isa. l. 4</reference>. (2.) To be just and impartial: <hi type="italic">Judge righteously.</hi> Judgment must be given according to the merits of the cause, without regard to the quality of the parties. The natives must not be suffered to abuse the strangers any more that the strangers to insult the natives or to encroach upon them; the great must not be suffered to oppress the small, nor to crush them, any more than the small, to rob the great, or to affront them. No faces must be known in judgment, but unbribed unbiased equity must always pass sentence. (3.) To be resolute and courageous: "<hi type="italic">You shall not be afraid of the face of man;</hi> be not overawed to do an ill thing, either by the clamours of the crowd or by the menaces of those that have power in their hands." And he gave them a good reason to enforce this charge: "<hi type="italic">For the judgment is God's.</hi> You are God's vicegerents, you act for him, and therefore must act like him; you are his representatives, but if you judge unrighteously, you misrepresent him. The judgment is his, and therefore he will protect you in doing right, and will certainly call you to account if you do wrong." <div eID="gen3369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3370" type="x-p"/> 3. He allowed them to bring all difficult cases to him, and he would always be ready to hear and determine, and to make both the judges and the people easy. <hi type="italic">Happy art thou. O Israel!</hi> in such praise as Moses was.
entries.3bd83f7ed638831a82861d880110b3d71c48c23d: <div eID="gen3370" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Israel's Sin at Kadesh. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1451.)</title> <div sID="gen3371" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">19</hi> And when we departed from Horeb, we went through all that great and terrible wilderness, which ye saw by the way of the mountain of the Amorites, as the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> our God commanded us; and we came to Kadesh-barnea. <hi type="super">20</hi> And I said unto you, Ye are come unto the mountain of the Amorites, which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> our God doth give unto us. <hi type="super">21</hi> Behold, the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God hath set the land before thee: go up <hi type="italic">and</hi> possess <hi type="italic">it,</hi> as the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of thy fathers hath said unto thee; fear not, neither be discouraged. <hi type="super">22</hi> And ye came near unto me every one of you, and said, We will send men before us, and they shall search us out the land, and bring us word again by what way we must go up, and into what cities we shall come. 23 And the saying pleased me well: and I took twelve men of you, one of a tribe: <hi type="super">24</hi> And they turned and went up into the mountain, and came unto the valley of Eshcol, and searched it out. 25 And they took of the fruit of the land in their hands, and brought <hi type="italic">it</hi> down unto us, and brought us word again, and said, <hi type="italic">It is</hi> a good land which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> our God doth give us. <hi type="super">26</hi> Notwithstanding ye would not go up, but rebelled against the commandment of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God: 27 And ye murmured in your tents, and said, Because the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hated us, he hath brought us forth out of the land of Egypt, to deliver us into the hand of the Amorites, to destroy us. <hi type="super">28</hi> Whither shall we go up? our brethren have discouraged our heart, saying, The people <hi type="italic">is</hi> greater and taller than we; the cities <hi type="italic">are</hi> great and walled up to heaven; and moreover we have seen the sons of the Anakims there. <hi type="super">29</hi> Then I said unto you, Dread not, neither be afraid of them. <hi type="super">30</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God which goeth before you, he shall fight for you, according to all that he did for you in Egypt before your eyes; <hi type="super">31</hi> And in the wilderness, where thou hast seen how that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God bare thee, as a man doth bear his son, in all the way that ye went, until ye came into this place. 32 Yet in this thing ye did not believe the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God, <hi type="super">33</hi> Who went in the way before you, to search you out a place to pitch your tents <hi type="italic">in,</hi> in fire by night, to show you by what way ye should go, and in a cloud by day. <hi type="super">34</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> heard the voice of your words, and was wroth, and sware, saying, <hi type="super">35</hi> Surely there shall not one of these men of this evil generation see that good land, which I sware to give unto your fathers, <hi type="super">36</hi> Save Caleb the son of Jephunneh; he shall see it, and to him will I give the land that he hath trodden upon, and to his children, because he hath wholly followed the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">37</hi> Also the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> was angry with me for your sakes, saying, Thou also shalt not go in thither. 38 <hi type="italic">But</hi> Joshua the son of Nun, which standeth before thee, he shall go in thither: encourage him: for he shall cause Israel to inherit it. <hi type="super">39</hi> Moreover your little ones, which ye said should be a prey, and your children, which in that day had no knowledge between good and evil, they shall go in thither, and unto them will I give it, and they shall possess it. <hi type="super">40</hi> But <hi type="italic">as for</hi> you, turn you, and take your journey into the wilderness by the way of the Red sea. <hi type="super">41</hi> Then ye answered and said unto me, We have sinned against the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , we will go up and fight, according to all that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> our God commanded us. And when ye had girded on every man his weapons of war, ye were ready to go up into the hill. <hi type="super">42</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto me, Say unto them, Go not up, neither fight; for I <hi type="italic">am</hi> not among you; lest ye be smitten before your enemies. 43 So I spake unto you; and ye would not hear, but rebelled against the commandment of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and went presumptuously up into the hill. <hi type="super">44</hi> And the Amorites, which dwelt in that mountain, came out against you, and chased you, as bees do, and destroyed you in Seir, <hi type="italic">even</hi> unto Hormah. <hi type="super">45</hi> And ye returned and wept before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; but the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> would not hearken to your voice, nor give ear unto you. <hi type="super">46</hi> So ye abode in Kadesh many days, according unto the days that ye abode <hi type="italic">there.</hi> <div eID="gen3371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3372" type="x-p"/> Moses here makes a large rehearsal of the fatal turn which was given to their affairs by their own sins, and God's wrath, when, from the very borders of Canaan, the honour of conquering it, and the pleasure of possessing it, the whole generation was hurried back into the wilderness, and their carcases fell there. It was a memorable story; we read it <reference osisRef="Num.13.1-Num.14.45">Num. 13 and 14</reference>, but divers circumstances are found here which are not related there. <div eID="gen3372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3373" type="x-p"/> I. He reminds them of their march from Horeb to Kadesh-barnea (<reference osisRef="Deut.1.19">v. 19</reference>), through <hi type="italic">that great and terrible wilderness.</hi> This he takes notice of, 1. To make them sensible of the great goodness of God to them, in guiding them through so great a wilderness, and protecting them from the mischiefs they were surrounded with in such a terrible wilderness. The remembrance of our dangers should make us thankful for our deliverances. 2. To aggravate the folly of those who, in their discontent, would have gone back to Egypt through the wilderness, though they had forfeited, and had no reason to expect, the divine guidance, in such a retrograde motion. <div eID="gen3373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3374" type="x-p"/> II. He shows them how fair they stood for Canaan at that time, <reference osisRef="Deut.1.20-Deut.1.21">v. 20, 21</reference>. He told them with triumph, the land is <hi type="italic">set before you, go up and possess it.</hi> He lets them see how near they were to a happy settlement when they put a bar in their own door, that their sin might appear the more exceedingly sinful. It will aggravate the eternal ruin of hypocrites that they were <hi type="italic">not far from the kingdom of God</hi> and yet came short, <reference osisRef="Mark.12.34">Mark xii. 34</reference>. <div eID="gen3374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3375" type="x-p"/> III. He lays the blame of sending the spies upon them, which did not appear in Numbers, there it is said (<reference osisRef="Deut.13.1-Deut.13.2">ch. xiii. 1, 2</reference>) that the Lord directed the sending of them, but here we find that the people first desired it, and God, in permitting it, gave them up to their counsels: <hi type="italic">You said, We will send men before us,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.1.22">v. 22</reference>. Moses had given them God's word (<reference osisRef="Deut.1.20-Deut.1.21">v. 20, 21</reference>), but they could not find in their hearts to rely upon that: human policy goes further with them than divine wisdom, and they will needs light a candle to the sun. As if it were not enough that they were sure of a God before them, they must send men before them. <div eID="gen3375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3376" type="x-p"/> IV. He repeats the report which the spies brought of the goodness of the land which they were sent to survey, <reference osisRef="Deut.1.24-Deut.1.25">v. 24, 25</reference>. The blessings which God has promised are truly valuable and desirable, even the unbelievers themselves being judges: never any looked into the holy land, but they must own it a good land. Yet they represented the difficulties of conquering it as insuperable (<reference osisRef="Deut.1.28">v. 28</reference>); as if it were in vain to think of attacking them either by battle, "for the people are taller than we," or by siege, "for the cities are walled up to heaven," an hyperbole which they made use of to serve their ill purpose, which was to dishearten the people, and perhaps they intended to reflect on the God of heaven himself, as if they were able to defy him, like the Babel-builders, the top of whose tower must reach to heaven, <reference osisRef="Gen.11.4">Gen. xi. 4</reference>. Those places only are walled up to heaven that are compassed with God's favour as with a shield. <div eID="gen3376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3377" type="x-p"/> V. He tells them what pains he took with them to encourage them, when their brethren had said so much to discourage them (<reference osisRef="Deut.1.29">v. 29</reference>): <hi type="italic">Then I said unto you, Dread not.</hi> Moses suggested enough to have stilled the tumult, and to have kept them with their faces towards Canaan. He assured them that God was present with them, and president among them, and would certainly <hi type="italic">fight for them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.1.30">v. 30</reference>. And for proof of his power over their enemies he refers them to what they had seen done in Egypt, where their enemies had all possible advantages against them and yet were humbled and forced to yield, <reference osisRef="Deut.1.30">v. 30</reference>. And for proof of God's goodwill to them, and the real kindness which he intended them, he refers them to what <hi type="italic">they had seen in the wilderness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.1.31">v. 31</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.1.33">33</reference>), through which they had been guided by the eye of divine wisdom in a pillar of cloud and fire (which guided both their motions and their rests), and had been carried in the arms of divine grace with as much care and tenderness as were ever shown to any child borne in the arms of a nursing father. And was there any room left to distrust this God? Or were they not the most ungrateful people in the world, who, after such sensible proofs of the divine goodness, <hi type="italic">hardened their hearts in the day of temptation?</hi> Moses had complained once that God had charged him to carry this people <hi type="italic">as a nursing father doth the sucking child</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.11.12">Num. xi. 12</reference>); but here he owns that it was God that so carried them, and perhaps this is alluded to (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.18">Acts xiii. 18</reference>), where he is said to <hi type="italic">bear them,</hi> or to <hi type="italic">suffer their manners.</hi> <div eID="gen3377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3378" type="x-p"/> VI. He charges them with the sin which they were guilty of upon this occasion. Though those to whom he was now speaking were a new generation, yet he lays it upon them: <hi type="italic">You rebelled, and you murmured;</hi> for many of these were then in being, though under twenty years old, and perhaps were engaged in the riot; and the rest inherited their fathers' vices, and smarted for them. Observe what he lays to their charge. 1. Disobedience and rebellion against God's law: <hi type="italic">You would not go up, but rebelled,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.1.26">v. 26</reference>. The rejecting of God's favours is really a rebelling against his authority. 2. Invidious reflections upon God's goodness. They basely suggested: <hi type="italic">Because the Lord hated us, he brought us out of Egypt,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.1.27">v. 27</reference>. What could have been more absurd, more disingenuous, and more reproachful to God? 3. An unbelieving heart at the bottom of all this: <hi type="italic">You did not believe the Lord your God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.1.32">v. 32</reference>. All your disobedience to God's laws, and distrust of his power and goodness, flow from a disbelief of his word. A sad pass it has come to with us when the God of eternal truth cannot be believed. <div eID="gen3378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3379" type="x-p"/> VII. He repeats the sentence passed upon them for this sin, which now they had seen the execution of. 1. They were all condemned to die in the wilderness, and none of them must be suffered to enter Canaan except Caleb and Joshua, <reference osisRef="Deut.1.34-Deut.1.38">v. 34-38</reference>. So long they must continue in their wanderings in the wilderness that most of them would drop off of course, and the youngest of them should be cut off. Thus <hi type="italic">they could not enter in because of unbelief.</hi> It was not the breach of any of the commands of the law that shut them out of Canaan, no, not the golden calf, but their disbelief of that promise which was typical of gospel grace, to signify that no sin will ruin us but unbelief, which is a sin against the remedy. 2. Moses himself afterwards fell under God's displeasure for a hasty word which they provoked him to speak: <hi type="italic">The Lord was angry with me for your sakes,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.1.37">v. 37</reference>. Because all the old stock must go off, Moses himself must not stay behind. Their unbelief let death into the camp, and, having entered, even Moses falls within his commission. 3. Yet here is mercy mixed with wrath. (1.) That, though Moses might not bring them into Canaan, Joshua should (<reference osisRef="Deut.1.38">v. 38</reference>): <hi type="italic">Encourage him;</hi> for he would be discouraged from taking up a government which he saw Moses himself fall under the weight of; but let him be assured that he shall accomplish that for which he is raised up: <hi type="italic">He shall cause Israel to inherit it.</hi> Thus <hi type="italic">what the law could not do, in that it was weak,</hi> Jesus, our Joshua, does by bringing in the better hope. (2.) That, though this generation should not enter into Canaan, the next should, <reference osisRef="Deut.1.39">v. 39</reference>. As they had been chosen for their fathers' sakes, so their children might justly have been rejected for their sakes. But <hi type="italic">mercy rejoiceth against judgement.</hi> <div eID="gen3379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3380" type="x-p"/> VIII. He reminds them of their foolish and fruitless attempt to get this sentence reversed when it was too late. 1. They tried it by their reformation in this particular; whereas they had refused to go up against the Canaanites, now they would go up, aye, that they would, in all haste, and they girded on their weapons of war for that purpose, <reference osisRef="Deut.1.41">v. 41</reference>. Thus, when the door is shut, and the day of grace is over, there will be found those that stand without and knock. But this, which looked like a reformation, proved but a further rebellion. God, by Moses, prohibited the attempt (<reference osisRef="Deut.1.42">v. 42</reference>): <hi type="italic">yet they went presumptuously up to the hill</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.1.43">v. 43</reference>), acting now in contempt of the threatening, as before in contempt of the promise, as if they were governed by a spirit of contradiction; and it sped accordingly (<reference osisRef="Deut.1.44">v. 44</reference>): they were chased and destroyed; and, by this defeat which they suffered when they provoked God to leave them, they were taught what success they might have had if they had kept themselves in his love. 2. They tried by their prayers and tears to get the sentence reversed: <hi type="italic">They returned and wept before the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.1.45">v. 45</reference>. While they were fretting and quarrelling, it is said (<reference osisRef="Num.14.1">Num. xiv. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">They wept that night;</hi> those were tears of rebellion <hi type="italic">against</hi> God, these were tears of repentance and humiliation <hi type="italic">before</hi> God. Note, Tears of discontent must be wept over again; the sorrow of the world worketh death, and is to be repented of; it is not so with godly sorrow, <hi type="italic">that</hi> will end in joy. But their weeping was all to no purpose. <hi type="italic">The Lord would not harken to your voice,</hi> because you would not harken to his; the decree had gone forth, and, like Esau, they found no place of repentance, though they sought it carefully with tears.  <chapter eID="Deut.1"/> <div eID="gen3380" type="x-p"/>

entries.abb0ad442cf1869b76a9533dcf12ddd69dac4475: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1643"/><title type="x-ms">THE FIFTH BOOK OF MOSES, CALLED DEUTERONOMY.</title> <div sID="gen2197" type="x-p"/> Commentary by Robert Jamieson<div eID="gen2197" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">CHAPTER 1</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Deut.1.1-Deut.1.46">De 1:1-46</reference>. Moses' Speech at the End of the Fortieth Year.</title> <div sID="gen2198" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1643"/><hi type="bold">1. These be the words which Moses spake unto all Israel--</hi>The mental condition of the people generally in that infantine age of the Church, and the greater number of them being of young or tender years, rendered it expedient to repeat the laws and counsels which God had given. Accordingly, to furnish a recapitulation of the leading branches of their faith and duty was among the last public services which Moses rendered to Israel. The scene of their delivery was on the plains of Moab where the encampment was pitched<div eID="gen2198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2199" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">on this side Jordan--</hi>or, as the Hebrew word may be rendered "on the bank of the Jordan."<div eID="gen2199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2200" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the wilderness, in the plain--</hi>the Arabah, a desert plain, or steppe, extended the whole way from the Red Sea north to the Sea of Tiberias. While the high tablelands of Moab were "cultivated fields," the Jordan valley, at the foot of the mountains where Israel was encamped, was a part of the great desert plain, little more inviting than the desert of Arabia. The locale is indicated by the names of the most prominent places around it. Some of these places are unknown to us. The Hebrew word, Suph, "red" (for "sea," which our translators have inserted, is not in the original, and Moses was now farther from the Red Sea than ever), probably meant a place noted for its reeds (<reference osisRef="Num.21.14">Nu 21:14</reference>).<div eID="gen2200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2201" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Tophel--</hi>identified as Tafyle or Tafeilah, lying between Bozrah and Kerak.<div eID="gen2201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2202" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Hazeroth--</hi>is a different place from that at which the Israelites encamped after leaving "the desert of Sinai." <div eID="gen2202" type="x-p"/>
entries.16c7e4e37bcb729e170c26ce903fe49a22248b5f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1644"/><div sID="gen2203" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1644"/><hi type="bold">2. There are eleven days' journey from Horeb--</hi>Distances are computed in the East still by the hours or days occupiesd by the journey. A day's journey on foot is about twenty miles--on camels, at the rate of three miles an hour, thirty miles--and by caravans, about twenty-five miles. But the Israelites, with children and flocks, would move at a slow rate. The length of the Ghor from Ezion-geber to Kadesh is a hundred miles. The days here mentioned were not necessarily successive days [Robinson], for the journey can be made in a much shorter period. But this mention of the time was made to show that the great number of years spent in travelling from Horeb to the plain of Moab was not owing to the length of the way, but to a very different cause; namely, banishment for their apostasy and frequent rebellions.<div eID="gen2203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2204" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mount Seir--</hi>the mountainous country of Edom. <div eID="gen2204" type="x-p"/>
entries.cce1f1b9dbe27786c3b937eb0ab137292e0edfe8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1645"/><div sID="gen2205" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1645"/><hi type="bold">3-8. in the fortieth year ... Moses spake unto the children of Israel, &c.--</hi>This impressive discourse, in which Moses reviewed all that God had done for His people, was delivered about a month before his death, and after peace and tranquillity had been restored by the complete conquest of Sihon and Og. <div eID="gen2205" type="x-p"/>
entries.2dceaf6bdb18221505d736aa04ddf90001f5133f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1651"/><div sID="gen2213" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1651"/><hi type="bold">9-18. I spake unto you at that time, saying, I am not able to bear you myself alone--</hi>a little before their arrival in Horeb. Moses addresses that new generation as the representatives of their fathers, in whose sight and hearing all the transactions he recounts took place. A reference is here made to the suggestion of Jethro (<reference osisRef="Exod.18.18">Ex 18:18</reference>). In noticing his practical adoption of a plan by which the administration of justice was committed to a select number of subordinate officers, Moses, by a beautiful allusion to the patriarchal blessing, ascribed the necessity of that memorable change in the government to the vast increase of the population. <div eID="gen2213" type="x-p"/>
entries.8076b303451dee7327c9a916e4ff3da7b837a6fa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1653"/><div sID="gen2215" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1653"/><hi type="bold">19-21. we went through all that great and terrible wilderness--</hi>of Paran, which included the desert and mountainous space lying between the wilderness of Shur westward, or towards Egypt and mount Seir, or the land of Edom eastwards; between the land of Canaan northwards, and the Red Sea southwards; and thus it appears to have comprehended really the wilderness of Sin and Sinai [Fisk]. It is called by the Arabs El Tih, "the wandering." It is a dreary waste of rock and of calcareous soil covered with black sharp flints; all travellers, from a feeling of its complete isolation from the world, describe it as a great and terrible wilderness. <div eID="gen2215" type="x-p"/>
entries.620ac71425444acb07371a087b88fa8302c3f29c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1654"/><div sID="gen2216" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1654"/><hi type="bold">22-33. ye came ... and said, We will send men before us, and they shall search us out the land--</hi>The proposal to despatch spies emanated from the people through unbelief; but Moses, believing them sincere, gave his cordial assent to this measure, and God on being consulted permitted them to follow the suggestion (see on <reference osisRef="Num.13.1">Nu 13:1</reference>). The issue proved disastrous to them, only through their own sin and folly. <div eID="gen2216" type="x-p"/>
entries.fc754bad090415fed7b88d153dfee86f42f7713d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1656"/><div sID="gen2219" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1656"/><hi type="bold">34-36. the Lord heard the voice of your words, and was wroth--</hi>In consequence of this aggravated offense (unbelief followed by open rebellion), the Israelites were doomed, in the righteous judgment of God, to a life of wandering in that dreary wilderness till the whole adult generation had disappeared by death. The only exceptions mentioned are Caleb and Joshua, who was to be Moses' successor. <div eID="gen2219" type="x-p"/>
entries.f997916221049af20205363190d01196b04ac141: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1657"/><div sID="gen2220" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1657"/><hi type="bold">37. Also the Lord was angry with me for your sakes--</hi>This statement seems to indicate that it was on this occasion Moses was condemned to share the fate of the people. But we know that it was several years afterwards that Moses betrayed an unhappy spirit of distrust at the waters of strife (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.32">Psa 106:32</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.106.33">33</reference>). This verse must be considered therefore as a parenthesis. <div eID="gen2220" type="x-p"/>
entries.349534a77b167109b132f6424508ba44cf95c04f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1658"/><div sID="gen2221" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1658"/><hi type="bold">39. your children ... who in that day had no knowledge between good and evil--</hi>All ancient versions read "to-day" instead of "that day"; and the sense is--"your children who now know," or "who know not as yet good or evil." As the children had not been partakers of the sinful outbreak, they were spared to obtain the privilege which their unbelieving parents had forfeited. God's ways are not as man's ways [Is 55:8, 9]. <div eID="gen2221" type="x-p"/>
entries.acc9e767bddd9a019b87b475f39c1244689682b4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1659"/><div sID="gen2222" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1659"/><hi type="bold">40-45. turn you, and take your journey into the ... Red Sea--</hi>This command they disregarded, and, determined to force an onward passage in spite of the earnest remonstrances of Moses, they attempted to cross the heights then occupied by the combined forces of the Amorites and Amalekites (compare <reference osisRef="Num.14.43">Nu 14:43</reference>), but were repulsed with great loss. People often experience distress even while in the way of duty. But how different their condition who suffer in situations where God is with them from the feelings of those who are conscious that they are in a position directly opposed to the divine will! The Israelites were grieved when they found themselves involved in difficulties and perils; but their sorrow arose not from a sense of the guilt so much as the sad effects of their perverse conduct; and "though they wept," they were not true penitents. So the Lord would not hearken to their voice, nor give ear unto them. <div eID="gen2222" type="x-p"/>
entries.c529f4563b19030f3af70e51b315277946a80651: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1660"/><div sID="gen2223" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1660"/><hi type="bold">46. So ye abode at Kadesh many days--</hi>That place had been the site of their encampment during the absence of the spies, which lasted forty days, and it is supposed from this verse that they prolonged their stay there after their defeat for a similar period. <chapter eID="Deut.1"/>

entries.14c079d254352834fd8356b17ff545cf219e3130: <div eID="gen6348" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Preface to the Book of Deuteronomy</title> <div sID="gen6349" type="x-p"/> We have borrowed the name of this book, as in former cases, from the Vulgate Latin, Deuteronomium, as the Vulgate has done from the Greek version of the Septuagint, Δευτερονομιον, which is a compound term literally signifying the second law, because it seems to contain a repetition of the preceding laws, from which circumstance it has been termed by the rabbins משנה mishneh, the iteration or doubling. <div eID="gen6349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6350" type="x-p"/> It appears that both these names are borrowed from <reference osisRef="Deu.17.18">Deu 17:18</reference>, where the king is commanded to write him a copy of this law; the original is משנה התורה mishneh hattorah, a repetition or doubling of the law, which the Septuagint have translated το δευτερονομιον, this second law, which we, properly enough, translate a copy of the law: but in Hebrew, like the preceding books, it takes its name from its commencement, אלה הדברים Elleh Haddebarim, these are the words; and in the best rabbinical Bibles its running title is ספר דברים Sepher Debarim, the book of debarim, or the book of the words. Our Saxon ancestors termed it the after law. <div eID="gen6350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6351" type="x-p"/> The Book of Deuteronomy contains an account of what passed in the wilderness from the first day of the eleventh month of the fortieth year after the departure of the Israelites from Egypt to the seventh day of the twelfth month of the same; making in the whole a history of the transactions of exactly five weeks, the months of the Jews being lunar. The history is continued about seven days after the death of Moses; for he began to deliver his first discourse to the people in the plains of Moab the first day of the eleventh month of the fortieth year, <reference osisRef="Deu.1.3">Deu 1:3</reference>, and died on the first day of the twelfth month of the same year, aged 120 years. <div eID="gen6351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6352" type="x-p"/> As the Israelites were now about to enter into the promised land, and many of them had not witnessed the different transactions in the wilderness, the former generations having been all destroyed except Joshua and Caleb; to impress their hearts with a deep sense of their obligation to God, and to prepare them for the inheritance which God had prepared for them. Moses here repeats the principal occurrences of the forty years, now almost elapsed; shows them the absolute necessity of fearing, loving, and obeying God; repeats the ten commandments, and particularly explains each, and the ordinances belonging to them, adding others which he had not delivered before; confirms the whole law in a most solemn manner, with exceeding great and precious promises to them that keep it, and a denunciation of the most awful judgments against those who should break it; renews the covenant between God and the people; prophesies of things which should come to pass in the latter days; blesses each of the tribes, prophetically, with the choicest spiritual and temporal blessings; and then, having viewed the whole extent of the land, from the top of Mount Nebo or Pisgah, he yielded up the ghost, and was privately buried by God, leaving Joshua the son of Nun for his successor. <div eID="gen6352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6353" type="x-p"/> The Book of Deuteronomy and the Epistle to the Hebrews contain the best comment on the nature, design, and use of the law; the former may be considered as an evangelical commentary on the four preceding books, in which the spiritual reference and signification of the different parts of the law are given, and given in such a manner as none could give who had not a clear discovery of the glory which was to be revealed. It may be safely asserted that very few parts of the Old Testament Scriptures can be read with greater profit by the genuine Christian than the Book of Deuteronomy. <div eID="gen6353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6354" type="x-p"/> The contents of the different chapters may be thus briefly summed up: - <div eID="gen6354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6355" type="x-p"/> On the first day of the eleventh month of the fortieth year, after the departure from Egypt, the Israelites being then on the east side of Jordan, in the land of the Moabites, Moses gives them a brief recapitulation of what took place in the wilderness, from their leaving Mount Horeb till they came to Kadesh; Deuteronomy 1. <div eID="gen6355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6356" type="x-p"/> Their travels from Kadesh till they come to the country of the Amorites, with the defeat of Sihon their king; Deuteronomy 2. The war with Og, king of Bashan, with the dividing his land and that of Sihon among the tribes of Reuben and Gad, and the half tribe of Manasseh; Deuteronomy 3. <div eID="gen6356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6357" type="x-p"/> Moses exhorts them to observe the Divine precepts; threatens those who should violate them; and appoints Bezer, Ramoth, and Golan, to be the cities of refuge on the east side of Jordan; Deuteronomy 4. <div eID="gen6357" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6358" type="x-p"/> Repeats the decalogue, and tells the people what effect the publication of it had on their fathers, when God spoke to them from the mount; Deuteronomy 5. <div eID="gen6358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6359" type="x-p"/> Exhorts them to love God with all their heart, and promises them an abundance of good things; Deuteronomy 6. <div eID="gen6359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6360" type="x-p"/> Repeats the command to exterminate the Canaanites, and all vestiges of their idolatry; Deuteronomy 7. <div eID="gen6360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6361" type="x-p"/> Recites the many interpositions of God's kindness which they had received during their forty years' travel in the wilderness, and strongly exhorts them to remember those mercies, and not to forfeit a continuance of his favors by ingratitude and disobedience; Deuteronomy 8. <div eID="gen6361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6362" type="x-p"/> Shows them that they were to pass Jordan in a short time, and that God was about to bring them in, not on account of their goodness, but of his mercy; Deuteronomy 9. <div eID="gen6362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6363" type="x-p"/> Gives an account of the second tables of the law, which he made at the command of God; mentions their journey from Beeroth to Jotbath, the choosing of the Levites, and the necessity of having the heart circumcised; Deuteronomy 10. <div eID="gen6363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6364" type="x-p"/> Continues an account of God's mighty acts in their behalf, and shows the blessings which should come on them who kept his law, and the curse on those who were disobedient. The blessings to be pronounced on Mount Gerizim, and the curses on Mount Ebal; Deuteronomy 11. <div eID="gen6364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6365" type="x-p"/> Commands them to destroy all monuments of idolatry in the land, to offer the different offerings and sacrifices, and to avoid eating of blood; Deuteronomy 12. <div eID="gen6365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6366" type="x-p"/> Ordinances against false prophets, idolatrous cities, etc.; Deuteronomy 13. <div eID="gen6366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6367" type="x-p"/> Forbids their cutting themselves at funerals, recapitulates the law concerning clean and unclean animals, and exhorts them to remember the Levites; Deuteronomy 14. <div eID="gen6367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6368" type="x-p"/> Every seventh year shall be a year of release for the poor of usury; first-born, etc.; Deuteronomy 15. <div eID="gen6368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6369" type="x-p"/> Concerning the annual feasts, passover, pentecost, and tabernacles; the establishment of judges and officers; no groves to be planted near the altar of God; Deuteronomy 16. <div eID="gen6369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6370" type="x-p"/> Idolaters are to be put to death; difficult cases in equity to be referred to the superior judges; of a king and his duties; Deuteronomy 17. <div eID="gen6370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6371" type="x-p"/> All divination is prohibited. The grand promise of an Extraordinary Prophet. How false prophets are to be distinguished; Deuteronomy 18. <div eID="gen6371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6372" type="x-p"/> The laws relative to the cities of refuge, and how the intentional murderer is to be treated; Deuteronomy 19. <div eID="gen6372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6373" type="x-p"/> Laws relative to the carrying on of war; who should be sent back from the army, how they are to treat the Canaanites, and how they are to commence sieges, Deuteronomy 20. <div eID="gen6373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6374" type="x-p"/> How to make expiation for an uncertain murder; marriages with captives; rights of the first-born, etc.; Deuteronomy 21. <div eID="gen6374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6375" type="x-p"/> Things lost or strayed are to be restored to their right owners; men and women must not interchange apparel; improper mixtures to be avoided; of the tokens of virginity; adulterers and adulteresses to be put to death; Deuteronomy 22. <div eID="gen6375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6376" type="x-p"/> Eunuchs, bastards, Moabites, and Ammonites, are not to be permitted to enter into the congregation of the Lord. Harlots not to be tolerated; Deuteronomy 23. <div eID="gen6376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6377" type="x-p"/> Laws relative to divorce; privileges of the newly-married man: concerning pledges, wages, gleanings, etc.; Deuteronomy 24. <div eID="gen6377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6378" type="x-p"/> More than forty stripes shall not be given. If a man die childless, his brother shall take his wife. Of weights, measures, etc.; Deuteronomy 25. Different ceremonies to be used in offering the first-fruits; tithes. Of full self-consecration to God; Deuteronomy 26. <div eID="gen6378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6379" type="x-p"/> The words of the law to be written on stones, and to be set up on Mount Ebal. The tribes which stand on Mount Gerizim to bless the obedient, and those which should stand on Mount Ebal to curse the disobedient. Who they are that are to be cursed; Deuteronomy 27. <div eID="gen6379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6380" type="x-p"/> The blessings of those who are faithful; curses against the disobedient; Deuteronomy 28. <div eID="gen6380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6381" type="x-p"/> A recital of the covenant of God, made not only with them, but for their posterity; Deuteronomy 29. <div eID="gen6381" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6382" type="x-p"/> Promises of pardon to the penitent; good and evil, life and death, are set before them; Deuteronomy 30. <div eID="gen6382" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6383" type="x-p"/> Moses, being now 120 years old, delivers a copy of the law which he had written into the hands of the priests, to be laid up in the ark, and to be publicly read every seventh year; a charge is given to Joshua; Deuteronomy 31. <div eID="gen6383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6384" type="x-p"/> The prophetical and historical song of Moses: he is commanded to go up to Mount Nebo that he may see the promised land; Deuteronomy 32. <div eID="gen6384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6385" type="x-p"/> The prophetical blessing of the twelve tribes. The indescribable happiness of Israel; Deuteronomy 33. <div eID="gen6385" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6386" type="x-p"/> Moses views the promised land from the top of Mount Nebo, dies, and is privately buried by the Lord. The Israelites mourn for him thirty days. <div eID="gen6386" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6387" type="x-p"/> Joshua takes command of the people. The character of Moses; <reference osisRef="Deu.34.1-Deu.34.12">Deu 34:1-12</reference>. <div eID="gen6387" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6388" type="x-p"/> At the close of this book I have added a number of useful Tables, such as no edition of the Bible ever could boast, viz.: <div eID="gen6388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6389" type="x-p"/> Table I. A perpetual table, showing through the course of 13 lunar cycles (which embrace every possible variation) the day of the week with which the Jewish year begins, and on which the passover is held; as also the lengths of the months Marchesvan and Cisleu. <div eID="gen6389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6390" type="x-p"/> Table II. Containing the whole variations in the reading of the Pareshioth or sections of the law for every year of the Jewish cycle of 247 years. <div eID="gen6390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6391" type="x-p"/> Table III. To find, with the help of Table IV., the day of the week upon which any Jewish new moon or festival happens. <div eID="gen6391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6392" type="x-p"/> Table IV. To determine upon what day of the week any Jewish month commences for any given year; as also the day of the week upon which the Jews celebrate their principal fasts and festivals. <div eID="gen6392" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6393" type="x-p"/> Table V. Containing the order of reading the Pareshioth and Haphtaroth for 90 Jewish years, i. e., from A. M. 5572 to A. M. 5661, both inclusive, connected with the corresponding dates in the Christian Era, according to the Gregorian or new style. <div eID="gen6393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6394" type="x-p"/> Table VI. Containing the year of the Jewish lunar cycle, the golden number, the first day of the Jewish pass over, Easter Sunday, and the commencement of each Jewish year according to the Gregorian Calendar, a. d. 1812 to a. d. 1900, both inclusive. All concluded with an explanation of the preceding tables. To them succeeds A Chronology of the Pentateuch, with the Book of Joshua; or a Systematic Arrangement of Events from the creation of Adam, A. M. 1, to the birth of Peleg, A. M. 1757, and thence to the death of Joshua, A. M. 2561. This chronology includes two tables, viz.: Table I. The birth and death of all the patriarchs, from Adam, A. M. 1, to Rhea, son of Peleg, A. M. 1787. Table II. A chronology of ancient kingdoms synchronized with the sacred history, from A. M. 1757, B. C. 2247, to A. M. 2561, B. C. 1443. The whole so calculated as to prevent the necessity of having recourse to systems of chronology for historic facts in anywise connected with those mentioned in the Sacred Writings. <div eID="gen6394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6395" type="x-p"/> The great utility of these tables will, I think, be at once evident to every Biblical critic, chronologist, and antiquary; and for the immense labor employed in their construction the editor, no doubt, will have their hearty thanks. <div eID="gen6395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6396" type="x-p"/> Adam Clarke. <div eID="gen6396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6397" type="x-p"/> Introduction to the book, <reference osisRef="Deu.1.1">Deu 1:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deu.1.2">Deu 1:2</reference>. Moses addresses the people in the fortieth year after the exodus from Egypt, <reference osisRef="Deu.1.3-Deu.1.5">Deu 1:3-5</reference>; and shows how God had spoken to them in Horeb, and the directions he gave them, <reference osisRef="Deu.1.6-Deu.1.8">Deu 1:6-8</reference>. How, at the commandment of the Lord, he had appointed officers, judges, etc., to share the government with him, <reference osisRef="Deu.1.9-Deu.1.18">Deu 1:9-18</reference>. Of their travels in the terrible wilderness, <reference osisRef="Deu.1.19-Deu.1.21">Deu 1:19-21</reference>. The people's request to have spies sent to search out the land, <reference osisRef="Deu.1.22-Deu.1.25">Deu 1:22-25</reference>. Of their murmuring and rebellion when they heard the report of the spies, <reference osisRef="Deu.1.26-Deu.1.28">Deu 1:26-28</reference>. How Moses encouraged them, <reference osisRef="Deu.1.29-Deu.1.33">Deu 1:29-33</reference>. The displeasure of the Lord against them because of their murmurings, and his purpose to exclude them from the good land, and give it to their children only, <reference osisRef="Deu.1.34-Deu.1.40">Deu 1:34-40</reference>. How they repented, and yet, without the authority of God, went against the Amorites, by whom they were defeated, <reference osisRef="Deu.1.41-Deu.1.44">Deu 1:41-44</reference>. Their return to Kadesh, where they abode many days, <reference osisRef="Deu.1.45">Deu 1:45</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deu.1.46">Deu 1:46</reference>. <div eID="gen6397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6398" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen6398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6399" type="x-p"/> These be the words which Moses spake - The five first verses of this chapter contain the introduction to the rest of the book: they do not appear to be the work of Moses, but were added probably either by Joshua or Ezra. <div eID="gen6399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6400" type="x-p"/> On this side Jordan - בעבר beeber, at the passage of Jordan, i. e., near or opposite to the place where the Israelites passed over after the death of Moses. Though עבר eber is used to signify both on this side and on the other side, and the connection in which it stands can only determine the meaning; yet here it signifies neither, but simply the place or ford where the Israelites passed over Jordan. <div eID="gen6400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6401" type="x-p"/> In the plain - That is, of Moab; over against the Red Sea - not the Red Sea, for they were now farther from it than they had been: the word sea is not in the text, and the word סוף suph, which we render red, does not signify the Red Sea, unless joined with ים yam, sea; here it must necessarily signify a place in or adjoining to the plains of Moab. Ptolemy mentions a people named Sophonites, that dwelt in Arabia Petraea, and it is probable that they took their name from this place; but see the note from Lightfoot, Numbers 20 (note), at the end. <div eID="gen6401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6402" type="x-p"/> Paran - This could not have been the Paran which was contiguous to the Red Sea, and not far from Mount Horeb; for the place here mentioned lay on the very borders of the promised land, at a vast distance from the former. <div eID="gen6402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6403" type="x-p"/> Dizahab - The word should be separated, as it is in the Hebrew, די זהב Di Zahab. As Zahab signifies gold, the Septuagint have translated it τα χρυσια, the gold mines; and the Vulgate ubi aurum est plurimum, where there is much gold. It is more likely to be the name of a place.
entries.c772bcb34da3385f8ff598d258ae2d4868d83213: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen6403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6404" type="x-p"/> There are eleven days' journey - The Israelites were eleven days in going from Horeb to Kadesh-barnea, where they were near the verge of the promised land; after which they were thirty-eight years wandering up and down in the vicinity of this place, not being permitted, because of their rebellions, to enter into the promised rest, though they were the whole of that time within a few miles of the land of Canaan!
entries.567c3c1103b3e920fb0fa3b2bdcc004cacb92be5: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen6404" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6405" type="x-p"/> The fortieth year - This was a melancholy year to the Hebrews in different respects; in the first month of this year Miriam died, Numbers 20; on the first day of the fifth month Aaron died, <reference osisRef="Num.33.38">Num 33:38</reference>; and about the conclusion of it, Moses himself died.
entries.3a6f637ac75e9344bca00b18ae67911cc7437e4b: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen6405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6406" type="x-p"/> Began Moses to declare this law - Began, הואיל hoil, willingly undertook; to declare, באר beer, to make bare, clear, etc., fully to explain, this law. See the conclusion of the preface.
entries.86d76c3db5ced706c4b6e52107c9b28b70e5cfe0: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen6406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6407" type="x-p"/> Ye have dwelt long enough, etc. - They came to Sinai in the third month after their departure from Egypt, <reference osisRef="Exo.19.1">Exo 19:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.19.2">Exo 19:2</reference>; and left it the twentieth of the second month of the second year, so it appears they had continued there nearly a whole year.
entries.1b465f57f3a39bf1401534ae6d8ffc704669aa13: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen6407" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6408" type="x-p"/> Go to the mount of the Amorites - On the south of the land of Canaan, towards the Dead Sea. <div eID="gen6408" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6409" type="x-p"/> Land of the Canaanites - That is, Phoenicia, the country of Sidon, and the coasts of the Mediterranean Sea from the country of the Philistines to Mount Libanus. The Canaanites and Phoenicians are often confounded. <div eID="gen6409" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6410" type="x-p"/> The river Euphrates - Thus Moses fixes the bounds of the land, to which on all quarters the territories of the Israelites might be extended, should the land of Canaan, properly so called, be found insufficient for them. Their South border might extend to the mount of the Amorites; their West to the borders of the Mediterranean Sea; their North to Lebanon; and their East border to the river Euphrates: and to this extent Solomon reigned; see <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.21">1Kgs 4:21</reference>. So that in his time, at least, the promise to Abraham was literally fulfilled; see below.
entries.7117e428bf0ea8fd89e1d51ad1ee6000eba14e30: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen6410" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6411" type="x-p"/> Ye are this day as the stars of heaven for multitude - This was the promise God made to Abraham, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.5">Gen 15:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.6">Gen 15:6</reference>; and Moses considers it now as amply fulfilled. But was it really so? Many suppose the expression to be hyperbolical; and others, no friends to revelation, think it a vain empty boast, because the stars, in their apprehension, amount to innumerable millions. Let us consider this subject. How many in number are the stars which appear to the naked eye? for it is by what appears to the naked eye we are to be governed in this business, for God brought Abraham forth abroad, i. e., out of doors, and bade him look towards heaven, not with a telescope, but with his naked eyes, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.5">Gen 15:5</reference>. Now I shall beg the objector to come forth abroad, and look up in the brightest and most favorable night, and count the stars - he need not be terrified at their abundance; the more they are, the more he can count; and I shall pledge myself to find a male Israelite in the very last census taken of this people, Numbers 26, for every star he finds in the whole upper hemisphere of heaven. The truth is, only about 3,010 stars can be seen by the naked eye in both the northern and southern hemispheres; and the Israelites, independently of women and children, were at the above time more than 600,000. And suppose we even allow that, from the late discoveries of Dr. Herschel and others with telescopes which have magnified between 35 and 36,000 times, there may be 75 millions of stars visible by the help of such instruments, which is the highest calculation ever made, yet still the Divine word stands literally true: St. Matthew says, Deuteronomy 1, that the generations from Abraham to Christ were 42; now we find at the second census that the fighting men among the Hebrews amounted to 603,000; and the Israelites, who have never ceased to be a distinct people, have so multiplied as far to exceed the number of all the fixed stars taken together.
entries.7b54eaa5f62aec577fd3e3582b4e3fce1df525ab: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen6411" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6412" type="x-p"/> Take you wise men - חכמים chachamim, such as had gained knowledge by great labor and study. Understanding נבנים nebonim, persons of discernment, judicious men. Known, ידעים yeduim, persons practiced in the operations of nature, capable of performing curious and important works.
entries.98b517359b88cd00557fe5b31adce805e4fb31ae: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen6412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6413" type="x-p"/> Captains over thousands, etc. - What a curious and well-regulated economy was that of the Israelites! See its order and arrangement: <div eID="gen6413" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6414" type="x-p"/> 1. God, the King and Supreme Judge; <div eID="gen6414" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6415" type="x-p"/> 2. Moses, God's prime minister; <div eID="gen6415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6416" type="x-p"/> 3. The priests, consulting him by Urim and Thummim; <div eID="gen6416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6417" type="x-p"/> 4. The chiefs or princes of the twelve tribes; <div eID="gen6417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6418" type="x-p"/> 5. Chilliarchs, or captains over thousands; <div eID="gen6418" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6419" type="x-p"/> 6. Centurions, or captains over hundreds; <div eID="gen6419" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6420" type="x-p"/> 7. Tribunes, or captains over fifty men; <div eID="gen6420" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6421" type="x-p"/> 8. Decurions, or captains over ten men; and, <div eID="gen6421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6422" type="x-p"/> 9. Officers, persons who might be employed by the different chiefs in executing particular commands. <div eID="gen6422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6423" type="x-p"/> All these held their authority from God, and yet were subject and accountable to each other. See the notes on Numbers 2 (note).
entries.2715c6154d640155f806aecae2487b6c81989abe: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen6423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6424" type="x-p"/> Ye shall not respect persons - Heb. faces. Let not the bold, daring countenance of the rich or mighty induce you to give an unrighteous decision; and let not the abject look of the poor man induce you either to favor him in an unrighteous cause, or to give judgment against him at the demand of the oppressor. Be uncorrupt and incorruptible, for the judgment is God's; ye minister in the place of God, act like Him.
entries.45b25b47751cb23f91afd8ede5fb16a72612f376: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen6424" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6425" type="x-p"/> We will send men before us - See on Numbers 13 (note).
entries.658f9cf6f3c24b4beebdfa68aa6dc3cefdc642c1: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen6425" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6426" type="x-p"/> Cities - walled up to heaven - That is, with very high walls which could not be easily scaled. High walls around houses, etc., in these parts of Arabia are still deemed a sufficient defense against the Arabs, who scarcely ever attempt any thing in the way of plunder but on horseback. The monastery on Mount Sinai is surrounded with very high walls without any gate; in the upper part of the wall there is a sort of window, or opening, from which a basket is suspended by a pulley, by which both persons and goods are received into and sent from the place. It is the same with the convent of St. Anthony, in Egypt; and this sort of wall is deemed a sufficient defense against the Arabs, who, as we have already observed, scarcely ever like to alight from their horses.
entries.d5ca179e9c268a35ffdd73c738676e76de9a2c69: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen6426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6427" type="x-p"/> The Lord - shall fight for you - In the Targum of Onkelos, it is, the Word of the Lord shall fight for you. In a great number of places the Targums or Chaldee paraphrases use the term מימרא דיי meimera dayeya or Yehovah, the Word of the Lord, exactly in the same way in which St. John uses the term Λογος Logos in the first chapter of his Gospel. Many instances of this have already occurred.
entries.0059f38d887bc5e20d2da08f9fa21c4cc9931715: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen6427" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6428" type="x-p"/> The Lord - was wroth - That is, his justice was incensed, and he evidenced his displeasure against you; and he could not have been a just God if he had not done so.
